contentAreaContent.introduction:
Imagined San Francisco
BETA VERSION

This project collects the most significant maps in the history of San Francisco and makes them accessible to the public, as well as to researchers.  Imagined San Francisco includes not only maps of the city as it was, but also unrealized urban plans that show the city as it might have been.  Maps and plans are organized chronologically by era.  Each entry is accompanied by a brief essay that situates the object in its historic context.  Each map also features an opacity slider that enables visitors to fade maps in and out over one another, and over the modern and historic basemaps.  (The console for the basemaps appears in the lower right of the homepage.)  Many maps are also accompanied by pin layers that display historic photographs and architectural renderings.  The “maps and plans” tab (in the upper left of the homepage) displays all of the maps collected on the site, while the “narratives” tab displays a series of essays that provide a curated analysis of the maps and plans.

maps.post_title: Duflot Map of Port of San Francisco

metadata.description:
Eugene Duflot de Mofras, “Port De San Francisco Dans La Haute Californie,”Arthus Bertrand Publisher, 1844.

Source: David Rumsey Map Collection

In 1839 the French government sent an explorer named Eugène Duflot de Mofras to survey the Pacific Coast of North America.  Duflot’s account focuses on the contests between European nations to claim control of California, and suggests that the French should consider the possibility of establishing themselves there (Hittell, 98).  As with Beechey’s account [link to it] Duflot documented the precipitous decline of the Presidios and of the Mission system, but did so with a much more sympathetic tone towards the Catholic Spanish.  “For foreign writers to slander the Spanish clergy from whom they have received the most generous hospitality is indeed deplorable.  With typical English coldness, Captain Beechey and Mr. Forbes, men imbued with the intolerance of Protestantism, are inclined to ridicule and cast insinuations on the activities of the Fathers” (Duflot, 141).

Duflot arrived in San Francisco in late 1841.  He described a sleepy village: “Founded only a few years ago, it has at the outside not more than twenty houses, which belong exclusively to foreigners and are used merely as places to store goods coming in by ship” (Duflot, 227).  The description is striking considering that only eight years later gold would be discovered in the Sierra Nevada, and the population of San Francisco would increase 2400 percent in a single year.

Though no one could have predicted such a frenzy, Duflot did understand San Francisco’s great potential as a center of commerce, an observation that has particular salience in light of his description of the Presidio:

The fort has been so completely abandoned that a ship could easily send its small boats over the to the shores below and without attracting the attention of the presidio carry off the cannons that could be easily rolled down the cliff.  This point, furthermore, is too high to permit accurate firing on ships that pass below, for vessels come within range only at the neck of the bay, and batteries to be effective would have to be erected at a lower level (Duflot, 229).

Seven years later, it would be the Americans, rather than the French, who would take advantage of these inadequate defenses.

But Duflot’s sociological observations and military assessments took up only a fraction of his account of the San Francisco Bay.  He focused on describing the bay itself, and on offering navigational tips.  A comparison with Beechey’s 1833 survey shows that Duflot borrowed heavily from the Englishman’s map.  Duflot showed five structures in the village of Yerba Buena that do not appear on Beechey’s survey.  But the largest difference is in the northeast corner of the map where Duflot corrected Beechey’s error of showing the Carquinez strait as being fed by three rivers (Harlow, 373).

Further Reading:

Eugène Duflot de Mofras, Exploration du Territoire de l’Orégon, des Californies et de la Mer Vermeille, Exécutée Pendant les Années 1840, 1841 et 1842 (A. Bertrand,1844). [English translation.]

Neal Harlow, “The Maps of San Francisco Bay and the Town of Yerba Buena to One Hundred Years Ago,” Pacific Historical Review 16(4), November, 1947.

John S. Hittell, A History of the City of San Francisco and Incidentally of the State of California (A. L. Bancroft & Company, 1878).

maps.post_title: Beechey Map of San Francisco Harbour

metadata.description:
Frederick William Beechey, “The Harbour of San Francisco, Nueva California,” Hydrographical Office of the Admiralty, 1833.

Source: David Rumsey Map Collection

Frederick William Beechey’s navigational chart is the first map to employ modern cartography in a survey of San Francisco Bay.  It is thus the first map of San Francisco that can be said to be accurate, in the sense that it corresponds closely with satellite imagery.

In 1825 the British Royal Navy gave command of the HMS Blossom to Frederick William Beechey, and tasked him with exploring the Bering Strait.  Beechey was to “cooperate with the English arctic expeditions under Sir William Parry and Sir John Franklin” (Harlow, 372).  A secondary purpose of his voyage was “to improve the surveys of both [James] Cook and [George] Vancouver,” who had produced the first English charts of the West Coast of North America (Harlow, 372).  As the arctic winter settled in, the Blossom headed south, arriving in San Francisco Bay on November 6, 1826.

The Mexican War of Independence had concluded in 1821, and the new regime had a policy of accommodating foreign expeditions.  Mexican officials gave “every assistance” to Beechey and his crew, asking only that a copy of the chart be left with them upon the conclusion of their work (Beechey, Chapter XIII; Harlow, 372).  Beechey’s account of his stay contains many observations that are of use to historians, particularly his portrayal of the remnants of the Mission system, which he described with unsparing candor.  The “remaining inmates of the mission” in San Francisco, he wrote, “were in as miserable a condition as it was possible to conceive” (Beechey, 358).

After a nearly two-month stay, Beechey departed on December 28, 1826.  The British Hydrographical Office of the Admiralty published Beechey’s map in 1833.  (Derek Hayes’s Historical Atlas of California reproduces manuscript versions of the map from 1827.)  The historian Neal Harlow writes that the chart marked the dawn of the “modern period in the cartography of the San Francisco Bay” (372).  The process of georeferencing historic maps bears out this observation.  Attempts at georeferencing Vancouver’s survey, for example, produce images that are so distorted as to be unintelligible.  Beechey’s survey, by contrast, corresponds remarkably well to modern satellite imagery.  Subsequent surveys of the San Francisco Bay–like Eugene Duflot de Mofras’s 1844 map–relied heavily on Beechey’s work.  Beechey’s chart remained the most accurate until the US Coast Survey’s first map of 1853.

The only clear error on Beechey’s map is the Carquinez Strait, which is here shown to be fed by three rivers, labeled “Rio Jesus Maria,” “Rio Sacramiento,” and “Rio San Joachin.”  According to Harlow, this was the only physical area that Beechey’s party did not survey in person, relying instead on descriptions given to them by local officials.  Duflot’s map is clearly derivative of Beechey’s except in this detail, where he showed the Strait connecting to the “Baie de los Carquines” (today Suisun Bay) which was in turn fed by only two rivers, the “Río del Sacramento” and the “Río San Joaquín.”

Beechey’s map employed a number of place names that have since changed.  “Paps,” for example, is an archaic geographic term referring to breast-shaped hills, here Twin Peaks.  (The Spanish also referred to Twin Peaks as “pechos,” or breasts.)  Mt. Tam is here shown as “Table Hill.”  “Blue Mountain” describes the modern-day Mt. Davidson.  “Silver Hummock” appears to describe Pacific Heights.

Another notable feature of Beechey’s map is the road system connecting the Presidio, the pueblo of Yerba Buena, and the Mission.  The road between the last two settlements would eventually move to the south, becoming the Mission Plank Road, which defined the eventual course of Market Street, and the otherwise incongruous orientation of the South of Market grid.

Further Reading:

Frederick William Beechey, Narrative of a Voyage to the Pacific and Beering’s Strait (H. Colburn and R. Bentley, 1831).

Neal Harlow, “The Maps of San Francisco Bay and the Town of Yerba Buena to One Hundred Years Ago,” Pacific Historical Review 16(4), November, 1947.

Derek Hayes, Historical Atlas of California (UC Press, 2007).
Historic photographs showing features described on the 1869 Coast Survey of San Francisco.

Benjamin Buckelew, “Buckelew Plan,” City of San Francisco, 1847.

Source: Yale University, Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library

In popular discourse one will sometimes encounter the claim that William Marston Eddy produced the first street map of San Francisco, or at least the first street map based on accurate surveys.  The Eddy Survey was completed in 1849, but not published until 1852.  Jasper O’Farrell’s 1847 survey is also sometimes cited as the first accurate street map, though his map was never published, and only redrawn versions of it appear in the archives.  However, historians who have closely studied this question agree that the mantle of the first accurate street map should go to the survey produced by Benjamin Buckelew, a recent immigrant from New Jersey, and a future major property owner in the Bay Area.

In January 1847 the Alcalde (Mayor) Washington Bartlett officially changed the name Yerba Buena to San Francisco and commissioned Buckelew to survey the newly christened city.  Bartlett signed Buckelew’s map on February 22, 1847, making it the first official map of San Francisco (Mawn, 169).  (Because the mayor’s signature appears on it, the Buckelew map is sometimes referred to as the Bartlett Map.)  O’Farrell’s survey was completed six months later, in August 1847.  O’Farrell himself referred to Buckelew’s map as the first he had ever seen, and stated that he did not change the original survey, but only expanded it (Mawn, 169).

Historians believe that O’Farrell’s 1847 map was destroyed in the Great Fire of 1906. However, it was redrawn in 1849. This image is a photostatic copy of the redrawn version. It is the closest to the original known to have survived.  Source: San Francisco History Center, San Francisco Public Library.

“Imagined San Francisco” does not include a georeferenced version of the O’Farrell survey because no original survives.  Also, there is an imperfect consensus about the extent of the survey.  Historians and commentators have pointed to maps that resemble the 1849 Eddy map as the best approximation of the O’Farrell survey, but others have pointed to maps that closely correspond to the 1847 Buckelew map.  (See, for example, the works of Mawn and Sandweiss.)  Nineteenth-century chroniclers of San Francisco state that O’Farrell established Market Street, so it seems clear that his survey extended south and west of Buckelew’s (Hittell, 115).  Indeed, one version of the Eddy map outlined the boundaries of the original O’Farrell Survey with a pink line, and that line extended just south of Market Street.  Yet no original survives, and by all accounts, the Eddy map contains all O’Farrell’s additions, and expands upon them.

Comparing the Buckelew map to Vioget’s 1839 survey is instructive.  Buckelew was the first to rectify the rhomboid blocks created by Vioget, and to extend the grid beyond the original pueblo of Yerba Buena.  The impetus for this more orthogonal survey was to regularize and rationalize the nascent real estate market.  A comparison between the Buckelew survey and modern maps confirms that Buckelew did indeed establish the street pattern of downtown San Francisco, a pattern that would be greatly expanded by Eddy just two years later.

Further Reading:

Hudson Bell, “Benjamin R. Buckelew & the First Official Map of San Francisco,” Fern Hill Tours website, July 14, 2022.

metadata.description:
Utah Construction submitted two schemes.  The firm referred to this version as the “Standard,” or “Chevron” plan.

From the SFRA Architectural Advisory Panel, Mario Ciampi, “Evaluation Report: Redevelopment of the Golden Gateway,” 1960:

DEVELOPERS
UTAH CONSTRUCTION AND MINING CO.
HENRY C. BECK CO.

ARCHITECTS
ANGUS McSWEENEY
DONALD BEACH KIRBY
LOUBET & GLYNN

This scheme proposes the construction of 1700 apartments in 6 slablike reinforced concrete structures rising approximately 17 stories. These structures are arranged in a chevron plan about a strong axis with a shopping center located at the south end.

The scheme appears to be motivated by economic factors with an absolute minimum regard for visual and environmental aspects. It is evident that the intent is to reproduce the same plan six times in order to standardize construction and reduce fees. Despite this, the proposed rent schedules indicate the apartments will be very expensive. A greater variety of apartment types would also be desirable.

The chevron plan creates a disturbing conflict with the normal grid pattern of the surrounding city. The relationship of the apartment area to the freeway ramps, public garage and proposed office building is very poorly considered.

No logical design connection with these elements exists. The proposed axis has reason neither for beginning nor end. No attempt has been made to separate the pedestrian from the automobile and, in fact, saturation of the site by automobiles is invited. The choice of partial basement garage parking and extensive surface parking is, at best, a very indecisive solution to the problem.

The slab structures, with a relatively high density, allow a great deal of open space, yet these spaces are in no real way utilized as a joyful environment for people.

This is a static and oppressive scheme, completely at variance with the most significant considerations for the beginning of redevelopment in this area of the city. The proposal is very similar in character to public housing projects constructed in many parts of the country, and fails completely to provide an appropriate environment of charm and delight for our citizens.

San Francisco Redevelopment Agency, “Architectural Advisory Panel Evaluation Report: Diamond Heights, Red Rock Hill Competition,” San Francisco Redevelopment Agency, 1961.

Source: HathiTrust

N. C. Raab, “A Progress Report to the Department of Public Works on the Southern Crossing of San Francisco Bay,” California Division of Bay Toll Crossings, 1956.

Source: Internet Archive

Division of San Francisco Bay Toll Crossings, “Report to Department of Public Works on the Southern Crossing of San Francisco Bay,” California Department of Public Works, 1955.

Source: Internet Archive

The San Francisco Bay Bridge opened in 1936 and within one year it was handling 20 percent more traffic than the California Department of Public Works (CDPW) had projected; by the end of World War II the figure was 91 percent (CDPW, 13).  In response the Joint Army-Navy Board (JANB) began discussing a southern crossing in 1946.  The JANB would eventually endorse the idea, and in 1953, a state Assemblyman from San Mateo County named Richard Dolwig introduced legislation to move forward with the project (Adler, 33).  In 1955, the CDPW proposed the crossing presented here.  Even though the plan enjoyed support from the state government, JANB, San Francisco city government, and the governments of East Bay cities, the southern crossing would be short-circuited by the Navy, which announced that it had a secret plan to test seaplanes and would not approve the bridge.  Many versions of a Southern Crossing have been proposed since 1946, but the version shown here came closest to being realized.

Further Reading:

Sy Adler, “Infrastructure Politics: The Dynamics of Crossing San Francisco Bay,” The Public Historian, 10(4), 1988.

From the SFRA Architectural Advisory Panel, Mario Ciampi, “Evaluation Report: Redevelopment of the Golden Gateway,” 1960:

DEVELOPERS
PERINI-SAN FRANCISCO ASSOCIATES

ARCHITECTS
WURSTER, BERNARDI & EMMONS
DE MARS & REAY

This scheme contains 5 tower apartments of 22 stories each, and 3 slab buildings almost equal in height. Housing units total 2174. Maisonettes are planned over the roofs of garage structures. Park and recreational facilities are provided, as well as elevated garages and auxiliary surface parking. A public garage and office building are included in the proposal.

Agreement is unanimous that this proposal is exceptionally successful. The plan is remarkably sensitive with:

an intimate, yet urban, character. The basic concept

of combining high rise and low rise structures is convincingly presented. This proposal further succeeds in establishing a prototype solution for high density residential development of gridiron blocks, within the context of the city’s general pattern. This has special significance for future growth.

Elevating the pedestrian onto plazas which form the roofs of the garages, and which are connected together with bridges over the streets, is excellently conceived. This complete separation of people and vehicular traffic is fundamental to the life of the area. While achieving this separation, the automobile has not simply been buried, but has been granted its claim to streets of valuable access.

The scale of the buildings is good. The tower and slab apartment buildings, and the office building, are well composed with the nearby Financial District and Customs House. Buildings have been effectively moved back from the elevated freeway. This general separation from the inherent acoustical problems, glare, and motion of the freeway could have been further enhanced if the large surface parking lot were developed as a greenbelt or park. The handsome central park, with its focal position and ease of access by bridges, is excellent. The maisonettes are considered well related to the towers except that they are too numerous and perhaps should appear more anonymous. They also appear quite expensive.

The tower apartments and slab structures are not considered very well studied individually. Their color is rather garish and the balconies impractical. This is also true of the proposed office building. However, there is convincing reason to believe this would be resolved by further study. The suggestion has been made that other talented architects could well be employed to give these buildings more individual character and elegance of their own.

This proposal has generated great enthusiasm. The competence evidenced by its authors gives assurance of their ability to carry through to actual completion the eloquent concept they have presented. The pattern of relationships between buildings would be a fine extension of the city; and the warmth, intimate character and variety of form and space promise a delightful human environment.

“Redevelopment Areas” from San Francisco Redevelopment Agency, “San Francisco Redevelopment Program: Summary of Project Data and Key Elements,” San Francisco Redevelopment Agency, 1981.

Source: Internet Archive

Source: SFRA Architectural Advisory Panel, Mario Ciampi, “Evaluation Report: Redevelopment of the Golden Gateway,” 1960:

DEVELOPERS

KERN COUNTY LAND COMPANY
DEL E. WEBB CONSTRUCTION COMPANY

ARCHITECTS

WELTON BECKET & ASSOCIATES
LAWRENCE LACKEY

This scheme includes high rise apartment towers and low slab structures of 2200 units, with equivalent parking provided. The project also provides for town houses, shopping centers and other related facilities such as a spiritual center, exhibit areas and recreational facilities.

The authors of this project have made a serious effort to provide a total environment for its occupants. The physical, cultural and spiritual aspects of life, as well as the relationship of the occupants to the general surrounding environment, have been given serious attention. The automobile has been kept in its proper place and the pedestrian circulations have been elevated to form a complete separation between the two functions.

The general plan relates well with the city grid pattern. It does not, however relate well with the existing Customs House. Furthermore, certain buildings have been placed too close to the elevated freeway, which would result in an obnoxious conflict between heavy traffic and domestic life.

The general apartment area seems to have been worked out block by block with emphasis on charm and detail rather than as a unified whole, and there is a resulting lack of restfulness and serenity.

The interrelationship between high and low rise buildings is crowded and con-fused. The high rise apartment buildings appear more like office buildings than elements for living, and the unprotected balconies do not appear useful. While the concept of bridges between the various blocks is excellent, they should be more pronounced and stronger as architectural statements.

The office building has been very well studied in its relationship to the mall and public garage. There is some question, however, that it may be too high and out of scale with the surrounding financial district.

It is generally concluded that this scheme lacks a sufficiently strong philosophy or concept to provide order, clarity and a distinguished architectural and environmental statement.

Source: SFRA Architectural Advisory Panel, Mario Ciampi, “Evaluation Report: Redevelopment of the Golden Gateway,” 1960.

DEVELOPERS

SIDNEY LEIKEN ENTERPRISES
THEO G. MEYER & SONS

ARCHITECTS

JAN LUBICZ-NYCZ & ASSOCIATES

This scheme is composed of a single apartment building of cruciform plan with 33 stories stepped back from the center in striated slabs. This building contains approximately 2100 apartment units elevated over a park with parking garages below. A shopping and recreational center adjoins this central element.

The basic concept of this proposal is remarkably bold, dynamic and brilliantly provocative. A wonderfully large space in the downtown area is created and an excellent relationship with Portsmouth Square, Ferry Park, the public garage and Customs House is achieved. Located in a handsome park setting, the apartment structure is a strong sculptural statement endeavoring to capture the Telegraph Hill spirit of living environment. In concept, this structure may be said to be beyond the conventional wisdom of architecture today and would undoubtedly be a major influence on future architectural design.

The scheme, however, is decidedly preliminary in nature, with numerous inherent problems unexplored. A very serious question is raised as to the ability of achieving in final execution an excellence comparable to the original principles.

And assuredly, this outspoken structure would demand excellence in all detail.

Vehicular traffic is successfully separated from the pedestrian, and the apartments are generally very well removed from the freeway. The unit apartment plans are excellent and enjoy a privacy, a delight in the surrounding park, and magnificent views of the city and bay. The site planning of all secondary elements, how-ever, is quite weak.

The central apartment structure should lend itself to construction at reasonable cost and to apartment units of reasonable basic rentals. Vertical circulations for the 33 stories would, however, be extremely wasteful.

Despite the highly commendable freshness of this proposal, the design expression is a very personal one, largely lacking in the restraint of civic and social direction. This alone is cause for considerable concern. Moreover, there is a disturbing restlessness to the commanding structure which, together with its overwhelming scale, seems at odds with basic needs of a living environment.

This great scale, furthermore, seems particularly inappropriate to the scale of the city.

From the SFRA Architectural Advisory Panel, Mario Ciampi, “Evaluation Report: Redevelopment of the Golden Gateway,” 1960:

DEVELOPERS

EICHLER HOMES, INC.
DINWIDDIE CONSTRUCTION CO

ARCHITECTS

ANSHEN & ALLEN

This scheme proposes 10 high-rise apartment tower units linked together in a group of 4 large modulated slab-type structures. Basement parking is provided and the city street pattern is permitted to project through the residential area.

The shopping center is located under an apartment building at the south end of the site.

Basic to this proposal is the effort to recreate the characteristic informality of the city’s residential skyline. In this direction, the attempt at variegation and fragmentation of the building façades is refreshing as an idea but not successfully executed. The façades seem artificial in their endeavor to imitate a pattern which appears accidentally in the cityscape, and the repeating of this accident throughout the project contradicts its freshness. Furthermore, the buildings are actually corridor-type slab structures masquerading as separate towers. The vertical stripes, emphasized by color, create a very nervous and restless character which, when repeated in such large areas, becomes monotonous. The absence of sufficient variation between masses and voids presents a rather formidable aspect.

A very serious effort has been made to conceal the elevated freeway by the construction of an earth berm which could be handsomely landscaped, and a central recreation area has been provided to give an openness to the center of the site.

The casual treatment of the open spaces, almost like a private yard extended, seems, however, badly out of scale. There is no interconnection of the buildings with these spaces and no unity of the whole composition toward a single enjoy. ment of an open space. Little relation is made with the adjoining office building and public garage area and no suggestion is given of extension into, or integration with, adjacent areas of the city.

The separation of vehicular traffic and pedestrian traffic is not well worked out.

Placing the garages in the basements and keeping the principal pedestrian circulation at street level creates hazardous and undesirable conflicts between the families who would occupy the area and the heavy downtown traffic. These garages are further considered to be needlessly expensive.

The shopping center seems poorly placed under one of the towers. It is not centrally located nor properly expressed as a shopping center with its glamour, gaiety and special character. Furthermore, it would be in conflict with the apartments overhead and create problems within the tower structures.

At first impression, this proposal appears quite interesting and its central concept quite promising. Upon closer scrutiny, however, it fails that promise. A clear distinction exists between representing or recreating the character of a city and capturing the essence or spirit of that character. This proposal does not give assurance that it has made that distinction.

From the SFRA Architectural Advisory Panel, Mario Ciampi, “Evaluation Report: Redevelopment of the Golden Gateway,” 1960:

DEVELOPERS
BARRETT-DIVERSIFIED-LESSER-BRAEMAR

ARCHITECTS
DANIEL, MANN, JOHNSON & MENDENHALL
CORLETT & SPACKMAN

This scheme includes 9 high-rise apartment buildings, approximately 20 and 28 stories high, and a 30-story apartment building for elderly citizens, placed over the public garage. These structures spring from an elevated pedestrian plateau over the site at third floor height relative to the surrounding streets.

Two floors of parking garages and services are provided below this level.

Basic to the site planning of this proposal is the decision to ignore the city proper and relate the entire project to the freeway and harbor. This results in a very unhappy conflict with the surrounding grid pattern and a marked isolation of the project.

The pedestrian plateau is an imaginative idea with certain virtues. Three distinct levels of circulation connecting with the street pattern are created, and separation of vehicular traffic and the pedestrian is achieved. This concept could possibly be carried out in the development of surrounding areas as urban change and growth continue. The pedestrian plateau suggests, however, a bleak and barren expanse for a living environment, and provision of appropriate landscaping would present formidable considerations of structure and cost.

The shopping center is well placed and such amenities as recreation facilities have merit. However, the apartment buildings are located too closely to the elevated freeway and would be exposed to undesirable noise, night lights and confusing motion.

The high-rise apartment building for elderly citizens is most unanimously and emphatically rejected. This is particularly undesirable sociologically and psychologically.

The main structures, through their placement, size and consistency of height, somehow succeed in occupying even more space visually than physically. It would be difficult to see into or out of the canyons which are created. This prospect is made even more frightening by the absolute pervasiveness of ostentatious surfaces and bizarre forms. Projecting balconies are very exposed and would not be practical in this city.

Rather than gaining from, or lending to, the spirit of the city, this scheme loudly projects itself in sharp conflict with that spirit.

From the SFRA Architectural Advisory Panel, Mario Ciampi, “Evaluation Report: Redevelopment of the Golden Gateway,” 1960:

DEVELOPERS

SIDNEY LEIKEN ENTERPRISES
THEO G. MEYER & SONS

ARCHITECTS

JAN LUBICZ-NYCZ & ASSOCIATES

This scheme is composed of a single apartment building of cruciform plan with 33 stories stepped back from the center in striated slabs. This building contains approximately 2100 apartment units elevated over a park with parking garages below. A shopping and recreational center adjoins this central element.

The basic concept of this proposal is remarkably bold, dynamic and brilliantly provocative. A wonderfully large space in the downtown area is created and an excellent relationship with Portsmouth Square, Ferry Park, the public garage and Customs House is achieved. Located in a handsome park setting, the apartment structure is a strong sculptural statement endeavoring to capture the Telegraph Hill spirit of living environment. In concept, this structure may be said to be beyond the conventional wisdom of architecture today and would undoubtedly be a major influence on future architectural design.

The scheme, however, is decidedly preliminary in nature, with numerous inherent problems unexplored. A very serious question is raised as to the ability of achieving in final execution an excellence comparable to the original principles.

And assuredly, this outspoken structure would demand excellence in all detail.

Vehicular traffic is successfully separated from the pedestrian, and the apartments are generally very well removed from the freeway. The unit apartment plans are excellent and enjoy a privacy, a delight in the surrounding park, and magnificent views of the city and bay. The site planning of all secondary elements, how-ever, is quite weak.

The central apartment structure should lend itself to construction at reasonable cost and to apartment units of reasonable basic rentals. Vertical circulations for the 33 stories would, however, be extremely wasteful.

Despite the highly commendable freshness of this proposal, the design expression is a very personal one, largely lacking in the restraint of civic and social direction. This alone is cause for considerable concern. Moreover, there is a disturbing restlessness to the commanding structure which, together with its overwhelming scale, seems at odds with basic needs of a living environment.

This great scale, furthermore, seems particularly inappropriate to the scale of the city.

The first survey of the pueblo of Yerba Buena, 1839, by Jean Jacques Vioget, a Mexican national of Swiss descent and a tavern keeper.  The map does not align perfectly with the modern grid.  In 1846 the pueblo hired Jasper O’Farrell resurvey the town, and he found that “Vioget’s North was eleven degrees too far east.”

See Geoffrey P. Mawn, “Framework for Destiny: San Francisco, 1847,” California Historical Quarterly, Vol. 51, No. 2 (Summer, 1972), https://doi.org/10.2307/25157373

California Department of Public Works, “Report to the California Toll Bridge Authority Covering Preliminary Studies for an Additional Bridge between San Francisco and the East Bay Metropolitan Area,” California State Printing Office, 1947, Plate V-8.

Source: Archive.org

The San Francisco Bay Bridge opened in 1936.  From 1939 to 1958 the upper deck carried vehicular traffic, while the lower deck was devoted to passenger rail.  By the end of World War II, the bridge was handling 91 percent more traffic than the California Department of Public Works (CDPW) had anticipated.  By the time the CDPW published its 1947 report, traffic had reached a volume not projected until 1970 (CDPW, 13).  The map presented here shows 11 proposals that the report analyzed.  The general aim of the proposals was to ease congestion and promote economic development without running afoul of maritime shipping interests or the United States military, which still had a substantial presence in the Bay Area.  Though dozens of stakeholders put forward dozens of variations on these proposals, this map shows the main ideas that were debated from the 1940s to the 1970s.

The proposals are numbered from 1 to 12 on the map, with 1 describing the original Bay Bridge.  The report evaluated the proposals based on traffic patterns, vertical clearance for maritime navigation, rail infrastructure, soil quality for bridgeheads, and cost.  The CDPW offered no formal recommendations, but an attentive reader would have found abundant support for a bridge very near the existing one, which was already in “the most favorable location” (97).  The report argued that “no location other than one in close proximity to the existing bridge is likely to divert anything like half the traffic now using the San Francisco-Oakland Bay bridge” (CDPW, 18).  However, the CDPW was only one of a host of stakeholders.  In the postwar period, a vigorous debate was had between interests on both sides of the bay.  City governments, chambers of commerce, and labor unions fought it out in the pages of the local press, as well as in state legislative hearings and with the Joint Army-Navy Board (JANB).

To summarize, the proposals that terminated on Telegraph Hill (labeled 2-4 and 6 and 7) never received serious consideration from major stakeholders.  There were a variety of reasons for this, but the most salient were the density of settlement and narrowness of streets in that part of San Francisco.  These conditions meant that the capacity of any northern crossing would have to be limited, guaranteeing that the bridge would be less effective at easing congestion.  But either a southern crossing (proposals 10-12) or a second bridge that ran parallel to the existing one (labeled 8 and 9) would likely be more effective in that regard.  And indeed, the local debate revolved around those options.

The planning historian Sy Adler has shown in detail how complex and occasionally capricious the politics of crossing the bay were.  But some patterns are discernible.  In general, the Oakland city government and business community favored a parallel crossing because it would ensure the economic centrality of Oakland in the East Bay.  Though the CDPW’s 1947 report offered no recommendations, it did note that the location of the existing bridge was ideal–if a bridge had not already exist, one would need to have been built on that site.   Cities to the south, like San Leandro and especially Hayward, favored a southern crossing since the investment would allow those cities more independence from their larger neighbor.  San Franciscans favored different proposals at different moments.  One of the principal aims of the city government and the business community was to compete with Oakland and the South Bay for the western termini of the major freight lines.  The southern waterfront was much better suited to rail yards than was downtown or South of Market, so San Franciscans favored a southern crossing.  However, once it became clear that the Southern Pacific, Western Pacific, and Santa Fé had no intention of moving their termini to San Francisco, the locals switched their support back to a parallel crossing.

However, both options would eventually be thwarted by the military.  In its own 1947 report, the JANB invoked civil defense.  The parallel crossing violated the principle of dispersion: building major bridges too close to one another meant that both could be taken out with a single attack.  Partly because the parallel crossing was unacceptable, the JANB did in fact support the southern crossing in 1947.  However, the Navy pulled the rug out from under the proposal in 1949 because it had “plans for possible seaplane development.”  Adler reports that these “plans were so new and so secret that the Bay Area navy official who made public the opposition did not know any of the details. This was a decision taken at the top level of the navy command in Washington; the local navy people were as surprised as everyone else” (Adler, 35).  For the moment at least, both the parallel and southern crossing plans were dead.

The failure of the two proposals with the most local support did, however, create the conditions where a third option could emerge.  In addition to supporting a southern crossing, the 1947 JANB report also argued that the Bay Area’s transportation problems could not be solved only with private vehicles.  The obvious solution was a regional rail rapid transit system, with an underwater tube connecting Oakland and San Francisco (Adler, 26).  This solution would have the additional benefit of freeing the lower deck of the existing bridge from rail service, thereby doubling its capacity for vehicular traffic (Adler, 27).  JANB believed that this tube should run close to the southern crossing, which terminated at Army Street in San Francisco, and 5th Street in Alameda (a route almost identical to proposal 12 here) (Congressional Record, 1947, A567).  In the 1950s, interests in San Francisco and Oakland would coalesce around this plan but favored a route much closer to the CPDW’s tube (proposal 5 here) that would connect the two downtowns.  This coalition was the driving force behind the eventual creation of the Bay Area Rapid Transit (BART) system.

Further Reading:

Sy Adler, “Infrastructure Politics: The Dynamics of Crossing San Francisco Bay,” The Public Historian, 10(4), 1988.

Source: Internet Archive

The Golden Gate Bridge opened in 1937, and like the Bay Bridge, it quickly exceeded its projected capacity.  The present map shows the main proposals that the California Department of Public Works and the California Division of Toll Crossings (CDPW and CDTC) considered to address the traffic problems between San Francisco and Marin County.  While the report discussed all the options shown, it quickly dispensed with about half of them.

The authors considered the Point Bonita Bridge impractical.  While it would provide access to areas of southwestern Marin where they expected future residential development, the route would not do enough to relieve existing congestion.  The authors expected resistance from preservationists who were concerned about the Marin Headlands.  The suspension span would have to have been 2.5 miles, and considering the exposure to the open sea, the construction challenges would have been formidable.  Finally, to effectively connect the route to downtown, the scheme would require a freeway that “would traverse extensive residential areas and probably result in opposition from the City of San Francisco” (CDPW and CDTC, 23).

The report found that the approaches to the Point Cavallo Bridge would render that scheme impractical, too.  In Marin, the ramps would need to have been constructed on steep slopes, and would have required a major widening of Highway 101.  In San Francisco, the flat terrain in Crissy Field and the Presidio would have required the use of eminent domain for a swath of surrounding properties to attain the necessary grades.  Moreover, the close proximity to the Golden Gate Bridge would likely be “detrimental to the esthetic beauty” of the Bay, and so would likely face resistance from early environmentalists (CDPW and CDTC, 24).

The report did not consider the East Bay Viaduct in any depth, either, because the authors determined that it would have no effect on the traffic between San Francisco and Marin.  As for the subaqueous tubes, “many of the routes through the area studied encounter water of excessive depth. There also are areas with exposed rock on the Bay floor. This would require costly protective facilities for the tube” (25).  The report considered only one transit tunnel (labeled T-3 on the map), and one vehicular tunnel (labeled T-5), both beginning from Aquatic Park in San Francisco.

In general, the report advocated for public transit but made clear that any rail system would require subsidies, and that capacity for private vehicular traffic must be expanded first (CDPW and CDTC, 97).  Public transit options would likely include busses, ferries, and possibly rail, but the report was creative in its consideration of other possibilities.  Though it acknowledged that non-traditional modes could only be a small part of the solution, the report nonetheless considered hydrofoil, hovercraft, vertical or short take-off and landing (V/STOL) aircraft, helicopters, helicopter-carried busses, and gravity-vacuum (pneumatic) tubes.

A helicopter-carried bus as a public transportation option. Source: CDPW and CDTC, “San Francisco-Marin Crossing,” 1967, 20.

Vacuum Tube (pneumatic) public transportation proposal. Source: CDPW and CDTC, “San Francisco-Marin Crossing,” 1967, 21.

However, a second deck for the Golden Gate Bridge was the priority.  According to the report, this was the quickest and most economical way to expand private-vehicle capacity and to accommodate busses.  For structural reasons, the report considered Bay Area Rapid Transit (BART) on the second deck of the Golden Gate Bridge to be a non-starter (CDPW and CDTC, 24).  However, a tube that extended the nascent BART system into Marin might be considered in a subsequent phase of development.  But as it would strain available finance options a BART tube should only be considered once the capacity for private vehicles had been addressed (CDPW and CDTC, 109-110).

Early discussions of the BART system considered the possibility of including rail on the Golden Gate Bridge. The CDPW and CDTC report asserted that the idea was not structurally feasible, and so only considered vehicular traffic on a proposed second deck (24). Source: GE advertisement in Holiday Magazine, April 1961. (Image courtesy of Erica Fischer.)

The Golden Gate Bridge with a second deck accommodating one lane of bus-only traffic, as described by the CDPW and CDTC. The illustration comes from a report the following year elaborating on the plan. Source: Golden Gate Bridge District, “Golden Gate Bridge Lower Deck for Vehicular Traffic: Report on the Concept, Preliminary Design and Estimated Cost,” 1968.

After the second deck of the existing bridge was completed, the report suggested that Phase-II options might be useful.  The tube option labeled T-3 on the map was the only one that the authors considered appropriate for rapid transit, and the T-5 tube might be considered for vehicular traffic, though cost was a major concern with both these proposals (CDPW and CDTC, 25).  The bridge options that traversed Angel Island and terminated in Tiburon–the Fort Mason and Kearney Street bridges–provided “the best service and [would] develop the highest usage in 1990,” but they were not financially feasible without additional sources of funding (CDPW and CDTC, 109).  The report seemed to favor either the Point Diablo Bridge or the Twin Golden Gate bridge as Phase II options because they were more economical and they could rely on an expansion of existing infrastructure in San Francisco.

A combination of forces prevented any of the Marin Crossing plans from being realized.  Because financing for any of the proposals would have tapped revenues from the existing crossing, the Golden Gate Bridge and Highway District (the authority that managed the bridge) put up administrative roadblocks (Dyble, Chapter 7).  Over recent years, the emerging environmental movement had begun protesting projects that would alter the aesthetic qualities of the Bay or the Marin Headlands.  San Francisco was also one of the birth places of a nationwide freeway revolt, and since any new bridge would require a new freeway in the city, the political atmosphere of the late 1960s meant that any proposal would face opposition not only from the citizenry, but also from the Board of Supervisors.  By the mid-1970s, the proposals entertained here seemed well and truly dead.  Unlike plans for a Southern Crossing, which seem to reemerge every 10 or 15 years, the more ambitious Marin Crossings have all but disappeared from policy debates in the early twenty-first century.

Further Reading:

California Department of Public Works and Division of Toll Crossings, “San Francisco-Marin Crossing,” 1967.

Louise Nelson Dyble, Paying the Toll: Local Power, Regional Politics, and the Golden Gate Bridge (University of Pennsylvania Press, 2013).

William Issel, “Land Values, Human Values, and the Preservation of the City’s Treasured Appearance: Environmentalism, Politics, and the San Francisco Freeway Revolt,” Pacific Historical Review 68(4), 1999.

Raymond Mohl, “Stop the Road,” chapter from Mohl and Mark Rose, eds., Interstate: Highway Politics and Policy since 1939 (University of Tennessee Press, 2012).

Frederick Law Olmsted, “Plan for Public Pleasure Grounds,” in “Preliminary Report in Regard to a Plan of Public Pleasure Grounds for the City of San Francisco,” 31 March 1866.

Source: The Papers of Frederick Law Olmsted

Henry G. Langley, “The San Francisco Directory for the Year 1873,” S.D. Valentine & Sons Publisher, 1873.

Source: Internet Archive

Before google, and before the advent of the telephone book, the principal source of local information in San Francisco was the Langley Directory.  This 1873 fold-out map comes from the fourteenth edition.  Like the directories in other major American cities in the mid-nineteenth century, the Langley Directory was much more than a precursor to the phone book.  The directory is best understood as a combination of the yellow pages, booster pamphlet, and municipal report.  The directory contained not only the addresses of residents and businesses, but also this detailed map.  It also contained essays extolling the vitality of the local economy, and a host of data that would be reported in the municipality’s Annual Report by the end of the century.  Thus, Langley included descriptions of the structure of local government, as well as aggregate real estate assessments, property tax revenue, infrastructure expenditures, demographics, statistics on bonded debt, and so forth.

The map itself is notable in several respects.  This is the first map to show Columbus Avenue–here labeled as Montgomery Avenue, the Street Naming Commission changed it to Columbus Avenue in 1909.  This is also the first map to show Golden Gate Park.  Political boundaries are also represented on the map: the large numbers superimposed over downtown, South of Market, and the Western Addition indicate wards.  Labels on many of the wharves show which operations they were dedicated to.  See, for example, the “PMSS Wharf.  Steamers for China and Panama” at First and Townsend Streets.  Principal rail lines are clearly represented.  The main cemeteries are clearly shown, including the “Jewish Cemetery” that would later become Dolores Park. The map is also one of the first to present an imagined San Francisco: the extent of bay fill shows the unrealized aspirations of the local establishment.  A comparison to any modern basemap shows that Hunter’s Point, in particular, here extends much further into the bay than it ever would in reality.

James Butler, “Map of the City and County of San Francisco,” Britton & Co. Publishers, 1864.

Source: David Rumsey Map Collection.
Burnham submitted a scaled down version right after earthquake.  Had all the same stuff.

US Coast Survey, “Entrance to San Francisco Bay,” US Coast Survey, 1859.

Source: David Rumsey Map Collection

In 1859, US Coast Survey mapped the entire Bay.  The survey omits the interior of the San Francisco peninsula, and represents topography with hatching, rather than the more precise topographic lines.  The map also shows the built environment only selectively.  For example, the downtown area shows only a handful of buildings around Drumm and Davis Streets.  (The cartographer’s method for selecting which buildings to show is unknown.)  However, the map presents several notable developments since the 1853 survey.   Most prominently, the eastern shoreline shows the extension of the wharfs more than two blocks further into the bay in places.  The shoreline just south of Market Street also shows the establishment of new wharves.  In the area later to be named North Beach, Meigg’s Wharf was marked as “unfinished” in 1853, but appears completed here.  The 1859 survey is also notable in its representation of the Presidio.  The US military had established the complex as a base in 1850, but little was done to the site for more than ten years.  The map shows the settlement in idealized form, complete with the grid pattern as mandated by the 1680 additions to the Laws of the Indies.  However, only four extant buildings are shown at the complex, with perhaps an additional small outbuilding on the western edge–further evidence of the decay of Spain’s original military settlement.

US Coast Survey, “San Francisco Peninsula,” US Coast Survey, 1869.

Source: David Rumsey Map Collection.

The US Coast Survey’s 1869 map tracks the remarkable growth of San Francisco since the 1859 survey, but also shows that the pace of the development of the downtown shoreline slowed.  In fact, there appears to have been some consolidation of the wharf system just south of Market Street.  The 1857 and 1859 surveys show close to ten smaller wharves that do not appear in the 1869 survey.  However, the 1869 survey also shows two new larger wharves, one just south of the Market Street Wharf, and another extending into the bay from Howard Street.  The map also shows the earliest enclosure of Mission Bay, with a rail line on trestles.  The 1864 Butler map labels this line the “North & South Beach” Railroad.  The line extended from Fourth Street, south to the point that is labeled “Pt. of the Rocks” here but is labeled “Pt. San Quentin” in the other Coast Surveys.  Point San Quentin itself here featured four or five new wharves that connected to the new developments around Potrero Hill and the Mission District.  The rail line then extended south from Point San Quentin to the base of Hunter’s Point.

While the shoreline in the southern half of the city was steadily developed, the expansion of the city into the interior of the peninsula was dramatic.  The 1859 survey shows that was little built in the southern half of the city since 1853, excepting the cluster of housing around the Mission Dolores.  But by 1869 the Mission complex had densified considerably, and development now extended as far south as Bernal Hill.  A new rail line also wended its way through the nascent Mission District.  The 1857 and 1859 surveys show that development did not extend far west of Mason Street, but by 1869, the built environment extended to Divisadero Street.  The 1869 survey also shows the first road to transect the San Francisco Peninsula: the Point Lobos Toll Road–later renamed Geary Boulevard–now extended west to the Cliff House, overlooking the Pacific Ocean.

One of the most notable features of the 1869 map is that it provides a way to track San Francisco’s role in the Civil War.  In spite of its geographic isolation from the principal theaters of the war, San Francisco was key to the Union cause.  Shipments of gold from the Bay financed the Union Army and were a clear target not only for Confederate mercenaries, but also potentially for the British Navy, with whom military planners feared that the Confederacy might form an alliance.  While most Californians supported the Union, there was also a strong presence of Confederate sympathizers in the state (National Park Service).  All of these considerations led the US to fortify the shipping channels out of the Golden Gate.  In 1861 the Army stationed five officers and 100 men at the Presidio; by 1865 there were 50 officers and 1,360 men (84-85).  While the 1859 Bay Survey showed only four buildings at the Presidio, the 1869 Survey showed more than 50.  In addition to various small outbuildings, the new structures included barracks, officers’ quarters, hospital buildings, a chapel, a “stone magazine” for munitions storage, stables, and “laundresses quarters” (82).  A smaller military buildup can also be observed on Hunter’s Point, Fort Point, and Black Point, labeled “Pt San Jose” in the 1859 survey, and known since 1882 as Fort Mason.  A buildup is also visible on Alcatraz Island, which first became a prison–originally for military personnel–in 1861.

Further Reading

Kristin Baron, “The Presidio of San Francisco: An Architectural History” (National Park Service, 1998).

John Phillip Langelier and Daniel Bernard Rosen, “Historic Resource Study: El Presidio de San Francisco: A History under Spain and Mexico, 1776-1846” (National Park Service, 1992).

National Park Service, “The Civil War at the Golden Gate,” 2021.

Erwin Thompson, “The Presidio of San Francisco: A History from 1846 to 1995” (National Park Service, 1997).

US Coast Survey, “City of San Francisco and its Vicinity,” US Coast Survey, 1853.

Source: David Rumsey Map Collection

As San Francisco had become American only five years earlier (1848) this was the US Coast Survey’s first mapping of the city.  The numbers that appear in the Bay are depth soundings.  The dash-dotted line indicates the original coastline, while the double- and triple-dotted lines show 12- and 13-foot depths, respectively.  The map also shows that when downtown streets met the eastern shoreline, they continued into the Bay as wharves.  The 1853 Coast Survey is particularly notable in being the first comprehensive map of the built environment in the American period, showing the footprint of each structure in the city.  Most of the large buildings from Portsmouth Square to the shore were warehouses, evidence of the primacy of shipping to the economy of San Francisco.  Public Buildings are marked with capital letters (key appears in the upper-left corner).

A comparison to the Eddy Survey, from just one year earlier, is instructive in that it highlights the sometimes stark difference between plan and reality.  For example, the Eddy map shows the city extending southwest as far as Dolores Street, while the Coast Survey shows that this was a paper city: the extant settlement did not reach far past Fourth Street to the southwest.  Historians of nineteenth-century American urbanism have written about how plat maps served not only to guide the future growth of a city, but also to stimulate investment.  These plats were booster promotional material, suppositious cities meant to entice real estate speculators (Cronon, 32).

The Survey also holds the distinction of being the first accurate account of the city’s topography.  While the Sun Lithographic map (1850) uses hatching to show hills, cliffs, and dunes, this is the first to employ more precise topographic lines.  The large dunes around Third and Market Streets are shown here to have reached 80 feet in height–almost seven stories, taller in fact than many buildings near that intersection in 2024.  A comparison of the Survey and the Sun map shows the dune in a slightly different location.  Multiple accounts from the time describe the dunes as constantly shifting, so it may be that the Market Street dune shifted substantially in the three years between the two maps.  However, it seems at-least-as-likely that the Sun map is simply less accurate with respect to topographical features, given the gestural nature of the hatching.

In any case, these maps show a long-forgotten fact of life in early San Francisco: dunes dominated the landscape, and not only on the western half of the city, but also in the areas that would become downtown.  Market Street was not the central artery that residents from the 1870s-on would come to know because it was completely obstructed.  Heading southwest from the Bay, Market Street only spanned about four blocks before encountering a wall of sand around Sansome Street.  That wall was only the first aspect of a collection of dunes that extended to around Stockton Street, then the edge of town.  The dunes and the original coastline are perhaps the most disorienting features to twenty-first century San Franciscans, and those features were intimately connected.  Where did the sand dunes go?  Where did the material to fill the Bay come from?  Both questions have the same answer.

1850s photo of a sand dune being removed around 8th and Harrison Streets. Photo shows early San Francisco rail line loaded with cars full of sand. The “Hewes Steam Paddy Works” appears at the left. “Steam Paddy” was a derogatory term for a steam shovel, the implication being that the machine did the work that would have been delegated to Irish laborers. Source: FoundSF

Residents in the 1860s described the ceaseless activity of steam shovels as a feature of everyday life in San Francisco (Murdock, 108).  Historian Matthew Booker notes that “California’s first railroad carried sand, not passengers or freight.  It accomplished two tasks at the same time: filling up the unstable tidelands while removing unstable dunes” (Booker, 63).  Tracks for rail operations were temporary, moving to a new dune once one current one was leveled.  Rail operations represented enormous capital expenditures, but water-front property in San Francisco was the most valuable in the American West.  Early in the land rush, there are reports of newly filled water lots appreciating as much as 4300% almost immediately after purchase, while inland property that might formerly have been buried under dunes might only expect to appreciate 2000% in one year (Ryan, 277).  By the end of 1850, more than 770 water lots had been platted and sold, some of them still under “as much as 35-feet” of water (Booker, 55).

1855 view of water lots, marked off with posts in North Beach, with Alcatraz Island appearing in the background. All around the northern and eastern shoreline, the plat continued out into the Bay, creating lots awaiting fill and entry into the chaotic San Francisco real estate market. Photographer: G. R. Fardon. Source: Bancroft Library.

Finally, the Coast Survey is notable in being the first map in the American period to show the connection between the growing city and the original Spanish settlement.  The Presidio lay to the west of the surveyed area, so does not appear in this map.  But the Misíon San Francisco de Asís (Mission Dolores) appears in the lower left of the map.  Dating back to the Spanish period, the old Mission Road was the original artery connecting Yerba Buena cove to the Mission.  In 1851, an entrepreneur paved it with boards, and began charging a toll.  Thenceforth, the artery was known as the Plank Road, as it is identified here.  The connection to the Mission predated the American period and subsequent development responded to this pattern–the South of Market grid was oriented not North-South, but to the Mission Dolores (Ryan, 210, 296-297).

Detail of William Frederick Beechey’s 1833 map, “The Harbour of San Francisco, Nueva California,” showing the rough locations of the original roads connecting the Presidio, Mission, and pueblo of Yerba Buena. Source: David Rumsey.

 

Further Reading

Matthew Morse Booker, Down by the Bay: San Francisco’s History between the Tides (UC Press, 2013).

William Cronon, Nature’s Metropolis: Chicago and the Great West (Norton, 1991).

Charles Murdock, A Backward Glance at Eighty: Recollections & Comments (P. Elder & Co, 1921).

Mary Ryan, Taking the Land to Make the City : A Bicoastal History of North America (University of Texas Press, 2019).

Nancy Taniguchi, Dirty Deeds: Land, Violence, and the 1856 San Francisco Vigilance Committee (University of Oklahoma Press, 2016).

Works Progress Administration, “Model of San Francisco,” San Francisco City Planning Commission, 1940.

Source: David Rumsey Map Collection

The San Francisco model was built by the Works Progress Administration (WPA), a New Deal agency, in the late 1930s.  The model is made from wood, and measures 42 by 38 feet.  The scale is 1 inch to 100 feet.  The map presented here is a composite photograph of the 158 discrete pieces that comprise the entire model.  Altogether the pieces contain about 6,000 removable city blocks.  The model is based on Harrison Ryker’s aerial photographs, which were also commissioned by the WPA, and which appear as a composite basemap on Imagined San Francisco.

A close comparison between the model and the Ryker basemap shows that the model is mostly faithful to the aerial photographs, down to individual buildings.  However, there are some discrepancies.  These are largely explained by the fact that the model was intended to be used as a planning tool–it provided a way for planners to visualize the city and imagine its future.  For example, the area bounded by Geary Boulevard, Steiner, Ellis, and Pierce Streets appears as open space dotted with modernist housing blocks on the model, while the Ryker photographs show that the area actually contained dozens of houses and apartment buildings, consistent with the density of the surrounding urban fabric.  The model was not showing the city as it was, but as it was imagined by the San Francisco Redevelopment Agency.  The 1956 Western Addition A-1 Urban Renewal Plan (which appears under the Western Addition Urban Renewal map group) is almost identical to the model, suggesting that planners removed the original 1940 blocks and replaced them with blocks showing the new scheme.  Similarly, the large freeway ramps that run from Market and Octavia Streets north to Golden Gate Avenue do not appear in the Ryker photographs, but do first appear in the 1963 Downtown Design Plan, prefiguring the construction of the Central Freeway.

According to David Rumsey, the model was “first displayed in sections in the Golden Gate International Exposition on Treasure Island in San Francisco Bay in 1939. In 1940-1942 it was displayed in San Francisco City Hall. . . . In 1968, the downtown portion of the model became a research and planning tool in the Environmental Simulation Laboratory in the College of Environmental Design at UC Berkeley. The model has not been on public view, in its entirety, since 1942.”

Source: David Rumsey Map Collection.

(Map closely cropped to prevent inset illustrations and graphics appearing over modern streets that would have been underwater in 1850.)

The Sun Lithographic map was one of the city’s earliest and it was produced for essentially promotional purposes.  The map was published as a broadside by an arm of the New York Sun newspaper in 1850.  The owner of the paper, Moses Yale Beach, had purchased a ship called the Apollo for a speculative voyage.  Enlisting his sons Moses Sperry, Alfred, and Henry to oversee the venture, they carried retail goods and passengers to San Francisco in early 1849.  In September, the Beaches beached the Apollo near the Central Wharf, and slowly sold their cargo to the public.  The “Apollo Store Ship” appears in the map near the corner of Sansome and Sacramento Streets; a vignette published on the broadside appears in the “1849 View of San Francisco” below this map.  After the original cargo sold, the Beaches began advertising the ship as a rental property for storage space.  Correspondence shows that the Apollo never brought in the kind of rental revenue needed to break even.  The family entertained the notion that they might recoup some of their losses by chartering new voyages, but as the surrounding water lots were developed the ship found any potential path back to sea blocked.  Henry Beach wrote that “the way I worked and toiled on the Apollo property (I know it has shortened my life five years) has effectively cured me of speculation in this country” (quoted in Delgado, 72).  Any remaining hope that the business venture might be rescued went up in the flames of the conflagration of 1851.  Today the site of the Apollo store ship is occupied by the old Federal Reserve of San Francisco building, which was completed in 1924.

The Old Federal Reserve Bank, viewed from the corner of Sacramento and Battery Streets.  Source: Wikimedia Commons.  

Contemporaneous illustrations and the earliest photographs suggest that the Sun Lithographic materials present an accurate view of the city in all but one respect, which is explained by the commercial interest that the map represents.  Here the Apollo is the one-and-only beached store ship in the port of San Francisco.  In fact, the Beach family had a surprising amount of competition in this market.  Historian and archeologist James Delgado reports that by the end of 1850, there were dozens of storeships in the port; by the end of the Gold Rush, there had been hundreds (Delgado 61, 69).  Nor was the Apollo the first beached storeship.  In July of 1849, a former whaling ship, the Niantic, was run ashore on the west side of the corner of Sansome and Clay Streets.  As is clear from the present map, and from the 1852 Eddy survey, the Niantic site was closer to the original shoreline, and to permanently dry land.  An English visitor named Francis Marryat published a well known illustration of the Niantic site in 1855:

Francis Marryat, “High and Dry,” from “Mountains and Molehills, or Recollections of a Burnt Journal” (London, 1855).  Source: Bancroft Library.

This illustration shows the Niantic as it would have appeared after its conversion to a hotel.  Some commentators have suggested that the storeship on the left is the Apollo, though Marryat himself never says so, and the archeological evidence is clear that the two ships were blocks apart.  The General Harrison was beached a block to the east, on Battery Street, but the National Park Service studies show no other ship so close to the Niantic.  Marryat may have simply been taking artistic license, or it may be that these storeships were so abundant that not all were properly documented.  In any case, this entire landscape would be almost completely erased only a few years after it had been established, when the fire of 1851 swept through.

The Sun Lithographic map is also of interest because it shows the contours of the original coastline perhaps more clearly than any other historical map.  The neighborhood that is known as Mission Bay in the 2020s was once actual bay, extending as far west as modern Seventh Street.  The North Beach neighborhood was once defined by an actual beach, which extended as far south as Francisco Street.  Most of the modern Financial District was once in the bay, which extended as far west as Montgomery Street.  The blue lines that hug the coast describe the tidal zone as it existed in 1850.  The blocks that appear in the tidal zone show the area that was first developed as “water lots” or “tide lots.” (The numbered lots themselves are clearly visible in the Eddy Survey of 1852, and are discussed in the essay accompanying that map.)

San Francisco’s early topography is also first shown in the Sun Lithographic map.  The hatch lines describe features of the city that exist in the 2020s, like Nob Hill and Telegraph Hill, but they also describe features that were removed very early in San Francisco’s history.  Most prominently, the map shows the large sand dunes that blocked Market Street at Sansome Street, and extended into the South of Market District, and another group of dunes that occupied the area north of Market that is bounded by Sutter, Montgomery, O’Farrell, and Stockton Streets.  (These features are also described in the 1853 Coast Survey, and are discussed in the essay accompanying that map.)  The map also shows the steep bluffs that grew out of the shoreline and led up to Telegraph Hill.  The bluffs are visible in the modern Aerial Imagery basemap, but in some sections–as in the area just north of Vallejo Street–the modern bluffs appear almost a full block west of where they were in 1850.  This is because the bluffs became a quarry where workers removed up to 150 feet of material, pushing the cliffs back from their original site on shores of San Francisco Bay (Booker, 64).

Sun Lithographic Map overlaying modern satellite imagery. The heavy shadows in the center left of the modern visualization show where the bluffs of Telegraph Hill are located in the 2020s. The heavy to the right, in front of the tide lines, show where these bluffs were in the 1850s, before they were quarried.
