From the SFRA Architectural Advisory Panel, Mario Ciampi, “Evaluation Report: Redevelopment of the Golden Gateway,” 1960:

DEVELOPERS
LEWIS KITCHEN REALTY CO.

ARCHITECTS
SKIDMORE, OWINGS & MERRILL

This scheme proposes the construction of 2575 apartment units housed in 3 giant slab structures, 22 stories high. The buildings are grouped around a broad elevated plaza which houses the garages and a shopping center. This spacious plaza is connected to a 1300 car public garage beneath a landscaped mall. An office building is included in the proposal.

This is an eloquent and impressive proposal, boldly conceived and beautifully presented. It is an extremely monumental concept and if executed would be an architectural statement of grandeur unique in our country. There is exceptional virtue in its spaciousness, and in the creation of its great park. A civic development of this magnitude, immediately adjacent to a congested financial district

could, in many respects, be a great asset to any city.

This very magnificence in a residential environment, however, presents grave considerations. The very size of the three apartment structures is awesome and out of scale with the surrounding city. There is a giantism and somewhat inhuman character prevalent. While admiring the stature of the buildings, one seriously questions the reaction to living in them.

The formidable aspect of the great walls presented might somewhat be relieved by more penetration, or opening up, of the structures. The curved form of these structures seems poorly considered.

The central plaza housing the garages, with the shopping center sculpturally expressed in the form of a circular sunken garden, is particularly handsome, and very well related to the apartment building. The scale of the unsightly elevated freeway has been very well recognized, and the buildings are well composed with this existing element. Eliminating the very strong symmetrical approach from the freeway ramps to the public garage is especially noteworthy.

The pedestrian has been very well isolated from automotive traffic. This concept as presented might very well be continued in surrounding areas in the city’s future growth

The project is well related to the Ferry Park and to harbor development, but completely destroys all view of the bay from the opposite side of the city. The proposed office building is excellently located and is a real contribution to the project.

While the great open spaces here are especially appealing, it is greatly feared the autocratic nature of this scheme would mar the finer scale and sensitive setting that make this city unique.

Composite of “Map of Western Addition, Land Claims,” Sections I-V, 1858.

Source: David Rumsey Map Collection

Further Reading:

John Shertzer Hittell, A History of the City of San Francisco; and incidentally of the State of California, A. L. Bancroft & Co. Publishers, 1878.
Leiken Models showing how the project would have looked on the ground.

William Marston Eddy, “Topographical & Complete Map of San Francisco,” Cooke & Le Count Publisher, 1852.

Source: David Rumsey Map Collection.

The Eddy map is one of the most important in the history of San Francisco.  The survey established patterns that would guide the future growth of the city, while also documenting features of its past that would soon be erased by boomtown urbanization.

In 1849 the newly established municipality of San Francisco hired a US Navy officer named William Marston Eddy to survey the city.  This was the first survey of San Francisco in the American period.  Eddy’s was also the first survey to show the dramatic impact of the Gold Rush.  Most estimates put San Francisco’s population at 200 in 1846 and 1,000 in 1848.  This was a dramatic increase, but it paled in comparison to the boom that followed the discovery of gold in the Sierra Nevada.  Between 1848 and 1849, the population increased from 1,000 to 25,000.  By 1852 the figure was 34,776.  Buckelew’s and O’Farrell’s 1847 surveys were scaled to respond to the 500% increase in population but were inadequate to a 2,400% increase.  This explains why a new survey was needed so soon, and why it covered so much larger an area.  Eddy continued to expand and refine his initial survey, and the 1852 version of his map is presented here.

The city’s primary impetus for conducting the survey was to bring order to a chaotic scramble for land along the waterfront and to the west of the established city.  This scramble began in earnest shortly after the onset of the Mexican-American War in 1846 when the USS Portsmouth claimed San Francisco for the United States without firing a shot.  Thereafter followed a period of nearly two years, until the signing of the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo in 1848, when San Francisco was under American control, but was not yet American.  This circumstance created a legal limbo: was the city governed by Mexican or American laws?  Squatters and real estate speculators took advantage of the ambiguity, pressuring the ayuntamiento (city council) to certify land sales and create legal titles that might not otherwise have been approved.  In response, the ayuntamiento petitioned the “military-appointed Governor of California, General Stephen Kearney, for the right to sell” not only lands to the west of Yerba Buena, but also the “beachfront and tidelands” (Ferguson).  As the historian Laura Ferguson has noted, Mexican law reserved beach and tidelands for public use, while American law clearly designated such lands as property of the federal government (see also Dow, 84).  Yet Kearney gave the city approval to divide and sell so-called water lots in spite of the fact that this action almost certainly violated any and all laws that might have governed the circumstance.  This outcome likely would have been possible only in the interstices between national regimes, but not under either of them.

Legally or otherwise, the city now had the authority to sell land within its boundaries.  In 1849, the municipality had hired Eddy as a contractor to determine where those boundaries would be, and how the land within them would be subdivided (Booker, 50; Hittell, 150).  In 1851 the municipality hired him on a permanent basis as the City Engineer, and he continued to expand and refine his map.  The Eddy survey was a cadastral map, establishing street and property lines, laying out 1,400 new lots (Ryan, 272).  An artifact of the colonial period persisted in these surveys: the Spanish Crown had mandated that new territories be surveyed in varas–a unit of measurement equal to about 33 inches.  Richardson employed the vara in his original survey of Yerba Buena.  The Vioget survey standardized the lot size at 50 x 50 varas, and Buckelew and O’Farrell continued this practice.  The Eddy map shows how the most densely populated area of the city, around the eastern shoreline, had already been subdivided into lots of 50 x 16 varas, but with the new lots west of Montgomery Street Eddy employed the original unit of 50 x 50 varas.

There are at least half-a-dozen versions of the Eddy map in the archives.  All versions follow the Buckelew map precisely, except in switching the street names of Dupont and Stockton.  (Dupont was renamed Grant Street, after President Ulysses S. Grant, following the earthquake of 1906.)  “Imagined San Francisco” uses this version because it is the most complete.  Unlike earlier versions, the 1852 survey shows how some downtown streets continued into the bay as wharves, including Broadway, Pacific and Market Streets.  This is the first version to show the South of Market curve into the Mission grid to the south–indeed, this is the first map by anyone to show this peculiar feature of San Francisco’s street pattern.  The 1852 map is also one of the only versions that shows the land claims to the west of Larkin Street.  The 1858 Land Claims map shows how chaotic and conflicting these claims really were.  Eddy’s map brought order to this tangle of competing claims at least on the east side of the city.

While the 1852 Eddy map is the most complete, one earlier version merits discussion because it contains a feature that does not appear as such on the present map, and because the map played an important role in determining subsequent patterns of development.  Eddy’s “Red Line” map marked the boundaries of the city, past and future.   Not to be confused with the twentieth-century maps that assessed mortgage lending risk (often in a discriminatory manner) Eddy’s map featured two red lines: the inner line described the pre-contact coastline, while the outer line described the planned future extent of the city.

Detail of the 1851 version of Eddy’s survey, showing the inner red line describing the original coastline, and the outer red line describing the planned future extent of the city.
W. M. Eddy, “Official map of the City of San Francisco,” 1851.
Source: UC Berkeley Library Digital Collections.

Some of this land had already been filled, while some was platted but was still underwater at high tide.  All the area within the outer red line was to be under the control of the city, while any waters or future lands outside the line would be under the jurisdiction of the State of California (Dow, 84).  A comparison with modern maps shows that all the new lots that Eddy here described eventually did become land.  The only exception is two city blocks that appeared in the modern Aquatic Cove, at the northern termini of Polk and Larkin Streets.  While the red lines themselves do not appear on the 1852 version, in fact all the information is still contained in the present map.  The inner red line corresponds closely to the original coastline as described on this map with a dark line, while the outer red line corresponds perfectly to the blocky, outer dark line that here marks the boundary between land and bay.

The Eddy maps are also notable in that they are the first to show the so-called Lagoon Survey.  This small, disconnected survey appears at the northwest edge of the newly planned grid, but is tilted about 30 degrees westward.  The survey sits at the edge of the Washerwoman’s Lagoon, so named because several laundries were established there during the 1840s.  Surprisingly, there is no peer reviewed scholarship on the Lagoon Survey, but in his guidebook Rand Richards states that Eddy himself conducted the survey in 1847.  The Buckelew and O’Farrell surveys had already been completed, so why would the Lagoon Survey not be oriented to the expanding grid?  Richards and other commentators have offered a variety of possibilities.  The grid might have been oriented to the shore of the lagoon, the original coastline, or even the planned Market Street.  Whatever the case, the new grid would eventually subsume the smaller development.  The Lagoon Survey appears in the Coast Surveys of 1853, 1859, and 1869 as well as the 1858 Land Claims map and the 1864 Butler map.  The 1873 Langley Directory map is the first to document the erasure of the Lagoon Survey; it does not appear on any map after 1869.  In the twenty-first century, there remain only a few small traces of the Lagoon Survey.  Two dead-end alleys–Blackstone Court and Grenard Terrace–are oriented to the Lagoon grid.  These alleys, and the properties immediately surrounding them, are the only surviving remnants of the Lagoon Survey.

Further Reading:

Matthew Morse Booker, Down by the Bay: San Francisco’s History between the Tides (UC Press, 2013).

James P. Delgado, Gold Rush Port: The Maritime Archaeology of San Francisco’s Waterfront (UC Press, 2009).

Gerald Dow, “Bay Fill in San Francisco: A History of Change,” Masters Thesis, San Francisco State University, 1973.

Laura E. Ferguson, “A Gateway without a Port: Making and Contesting San Francisco’s Early Waterfront,” Journal of Urban History 44(4), March, 2018.

John S. Hittell, A History of the City of San Francisco and Incidentally of the State of California (A. L. Bancroft & Company, 1878).

Gary Kamiya.  2016.  “San Francisco’s Off-kilter First Suburb.”  San Francisco Chronicle, Dec 10.

Rand Richards, Historic Walks in San Francisco : 18 Trails through the City’s Past (Heritage House Publishers, 2002).

Mary Ryan, Taking the Land to Make the City: A Bicoastal History of North America (University of Texas Press, 2019).

From the SFRA Architectural Advisory Panel, Mario Ciampi, “Evaluation Report: Redevelopment of the Golden Gateway,” 1960:

DEVELOPERS
PERINI-SAN FRANCISCO ASSOCIATES

ARCHITECTS
WURSTER, BERNARDI & EMMONS
DE MARS & REAY

This scheme contains 5 tower apartments of 22 stories each, and 3 slab buildings almost equal in height. Housing units total 2174. Maisonettes are planned over the roofs of garage structures. Park and recreational facilities are provided, as well as elevated garages and auxiliary surface parking. A public garage and office building are included in the proposal.

Agreement is unanimous that this proposal is exceptionally successful. The plan is remarkably sensitive with:

an intimate, yet urban, character. The basic concept

of combining high rise and low rise structures is convincingly presented. This proposal further succeeds in establishing a prototype solution for high density residential development of gridiron blocks, within the context of the city’s general pattern. This has special significance for future growth.

Elevating the pedestrian onto plazas which form the roofs of the garages, and which are connected together with bridges over the streets, is excellently conceived. This complete separation of people and vehicular traffic is fundamental to the life of the area. While achieving this separation, the automobile has not simply been buried, but has been granted its claim to streets of valuable access.

The scale of the buildings is good. The tower and slab apartment buildings, and the office building, are well composed with the nearby Financial District and Customs House. Buildings have been effectively moved back from the elevated freeway. This general separation from the inherent acoustical problems, glare, and motion of the freeway could have been further enhanced if the large surface parking lot were developed as a greenbelt or park. The handsome central park, with its focal position and ease of access by bridges, is excellent. The maisonettes are considered well related to the towers except that they are too numerous and perhaps should appear more anonymous. They also appear quite expensive.

The tower apartments and slab structures are not considered very well studied individually. Their color is rather garish and the balconies impractical. This is also true of the proposed office building. However, there is convincing reason to believe this would be resolved by further study. The suggestion has been made that other talented architects could well be employed to give these buildings more individual character and elegance of their own.

This proposal has generated great enthusiasm. The competence evidenced by its authors gives assurance of their ability to carry through to actual completion the eloquent concept they have presented. The pattern of relationships between buildings would be a fine extension of the city; and the warmth, intimate character and variety of form and space promise a delightful human environment.

From the SFRA Architectural Advisory Panel, Mario Ciampi, “Evaluation Report: Redevelopment of the Golden Gateway,” 1960:

DEVELOPERS
TISHMAN-CAHILL RENEWAL ASSOCIATES

ARCHITECTS
JOHN CARL WARNECKE & ASSOCIATES
GARDNER DAILEY & ASSOCIATES
VICTOR GRUEN & ASSOCIATES

This scheme substantially includes 6 high-rise towers of 16 stories, 3 long slab-like lower buildings, 2- and 3-story town houses, and a central plaza and shopping center. Three large elevated parking garages and a number of small parks and plazas are provided. The office building and public garage are not included in this proposal.

There is unanimous admiration of this proposal. It is a sensitive and distinguished solution to a very difficult problem. The carefully studied plan integrates well with the city grid pattern. A variety, elegance and charm, so vital to city living, is apparent. This variety, however, is not without its conflicts.

The high rise apartment towers are exceptionally handsome and graceful. The slab apartment structures, by comparison, however, are of rather uninteresting design. They might well be improved with a more chateau-like character. If these apartments were planned to include low rental units, as opposed to the luxury rentals of the towers, occupancy would be brought into range of a greater number of people. The project would thereby become more marketable. Despite their beauty, some concern was voiced that the apartment towers might be more appropriate with greater variety of design.

The town houses give rise to particular concern. They complicate the project and appear too expensive to justify. The area claimed by these houses could be utilized to better advantage as open space for the several thousand occupants of the project.

Relationship with the Customs House and future harbor development is good.

Landscaping and separation of the site into small manageable land areas appears successful.

Inadequate consideration has been given the presence of the elevated freeway.

The project too closely approaches this highly undesirable element, whereas the provision of at least a greenbelt buffer would have alleviated this problem.

Considerable concern was manifest over the street pattern within the project.

Positive separation of the pedestrian and vehicular traffic has not been provided, and this is especially hazardous for families occupying the area.

The garages, however, are well placed. The central plaza, with the shopping center, is particularly well conceived.

The opinion was expressed that this team of architects clearly displayed the capabilities required to carry their proposal on to successful completion, creating an urban environment consistent with the character of this city.

From the SFRA Architectural Advisory Panel, Mario Ciampi, “Evaluation Report: Redevelopment of the Golden Gateway,” 1960:

DEVELOPERS

SIDNEY LEIKEN ENTERPRISES
THEO G. MEYER & SONS

ARCHITECTS

JAN LUBICZ-NYCZ & ASSOCIATES

This scheme is composed of a single apartment building of cruciform plan with 33 stories stepped back from the center in striated slabs. This building contains approximately 2100 apartment units elevated over a park with parking garages below. A shopping and recreational center adjoins this central element.

The basic concept of this proposal is remarkably bold, dynamic and brilliantly provocative. A wonderfully large space in the downtown area is created and an excellent relationship with Portsmouth Square, Ferry Park, the public garage and Customs House is achieved. Located in a handsome park setting, the apartment structure is a strong sculptural statement endeavoring to capture the Telegraph Hill spirit of living environment. In concept, this structure may be said to be beyond the conventional wisdom of architecture today and would undoubtedly be a major influence on future architectural design.

The scheme, however, is decidedly preliminary in nature, with numerous inherent problems unexplored. A very serious question is raised as to the ability of achieving in final execution an excellence comparable to the original principles.

And assuredly, this outspoken structure would demand excellence in all detail.

Vehicular traffic is successfully separated from the pedestrian, and the apartments are generally very well removed from the freeway. The unit apartment plans are excellent and enjoy a privacy, a delight in the surrounding park, and magnificent views of the city and bay. The site planning of all secondary elements, how-ever, is quite weak.

The central apartment structure should lend itself to construction at reasonable cost and to apartment units of reasonable basic rentals. Vertical circulations for the 33 stories would, however, be extremely wasteful.

Despite the highly commendable freshness of this proposal, the design expression is a very personal one, largely lacking in the restraint of civic and social direction. This alone is cause for considerable concern. Moreover, there is a disturbing restlessness to the commanding structure which, together with its overwhelming scale, seems at odds with basic needs of a living environment.

This great scale, furthermore, seems particularly inappropriate to the scale of the city.

From the SFRA Architectural Advisory Panel, Mario Ciampi, “Evaluation Report: Redevelopment of the Golden Gateway,” 1960:

DEVELOPERS

EICHLER HOMES, INC.
DINWIDDIE CONSTRUCTION CO

ARCHITECTS

ANSHEN & ALLEN

This scheme proposes 10 high-rise apartment tower units linked together in a group of 4 large modulated slab-type structures. Basement parking is provided and the city street pattern is permitted to project through the residential area.

The shopping center is located under an apartment building at the south end of the site.

Basic to this proposal is the effort to recreate the characteristic informality of the city’s residential skyline. In this direction, the attempt at variegation and fragmentation of the building façades is refreshing as an idea but not successfully executed. The façades seem artificial in their endeavor to imitate a pattern which appears accidentally in the cityscape, and the repeating of this accident throughout the project contradicts its freshness. Furthermore, the buildings are actually corridor-type slab structures masquerading as separate towers. The vertical stripes, emphasized by color, create a very nervous and restless character which, when repeated in such large areas, becomes monotonous. The absence of sufficient variation between masses and voids presents a rather formidable aspect.

A very serious effort has been made to conceal the elevated freeway by the construction of an earth berm which could be handsomely landscaped, and a central recreation area has been provided to give an openness to the center of the site.

The casual treatment of the open spaces, almost like a private yard extended, seems, however, badly out of scale. There is no interconnection of the buildings with these spaces and no unity of the whole composition toward a single enjoy. ment of an open space. Little relation is made with the adjoining office building and public garage area and no suggestion is given of extension into, or integration with, adjacent areas of the city.

The separation of vehicular traffic and pedestrian traffic is not well worked out.

Furthermore, it would be in conflict with the apartments overhead and create problems within the tower structures.

A clear distinction exists between representing or recreating the character of a city and capturing the essence or spirit of that character. LAWRENCE LACKEY

This scheme includes high rise apartment towers and low slab structures of 2200 units, with equivalent parking provided. The project also provides for town houses, shopping centers and other related facilities such as a spiritual center, exhibit areas and recreational facilities.

The general plan relates well with the city grid pattern. It does not, however relate well with the existing Customs House. Furthermore, certain buildings have been placed too close to the elevated freeway, which would result in an obnoxious conflict between heavy traffic and domestic life.

The interrelationship between high and low rise buildings is crowded and con-fused. The office building has been very well studied in its relationship to the mall and public garage. There is some question, however, that it may be too high and out of scale with the surrounding financial district.

It is generally concluded that this scheme lacks a sufficiently strong philosophy or concept to provide order, clarity and a distinguished architectural and environmental statement.

From the SFRA Architectural Advisory Panel, Mario Ciampi, “Evaluation Report: Redevelopment of the Golden Gateway,” 1960:

DEVELOPERS
TISHMAN-CAHILL RENEWAL ASSOCIATES

ARCHITECTS
JOHN CARL WARNECKE & ASSOCIATES
GARDNER DAILEY & ASSOCIATES
VICTOR GRUEN & ASSOCIATES

This scheme substantially includes 6 high-rise towers of 16 stories, 3 long slab-like lower buildings, 2- and 3-story town houses, and a central plaza and shopping center. Three large elevated parking garages and a number of small parks and plazas are provided. The office building and public garage are not included in this proposal.

There is unanimous admiration of this proposal. It is a sensitive and distinguished solution to a very difficult problem. The carefully studied plan integrates well with the city grid pattern. A variety, elegance and charm, so vital to city living, is apparent. This variety, however, is not without its conflicts.

The high rise apartment towers are exceptionally handsome and graceful. The slab apartment structures, by comparison, however, are of rather uninteresting design. They might well be improved with a more chateau-like character. If these apartments were planned to include low rental units, as opposed to the luxury rentals of the towers, occupancy would be brought into range of a greater number of people. The project would thereby become more marketable. Despite their beauty, some concern was voiced that the apartment towers might be more appropriate with greater variety of design.

The town houses give rise to particular concern. They complicate the project and appear too expensive to justify. The area claimed by these houses could be utilized to better advantage as open space for the several thousand occupants of the project.

Relationship with the Customs House and future harbor development is good.

Landscaping and separation of the site into small manageable land areas appears successful.

Inadequate consideration has been given the presence of the elevated freeway.

The project too closely approaches this highly undesirable element, whereas the provision of at least a greenbelt buffer would have alleviated this problem.

Considerable concern was manifest over the street pattern within the project.

Positive separation of the pedestrian and vehicular traffic has not been provided, and this is especially hazardous for families occupying the area.

The garages, however, are well placed. The central plaza, with the shopping center, is particularly well conceived.

The opinion was expressed that this team of architects clearly displayed the capabilities required to carry their proposal on to successful completion, creating an urban environment consistent with the character of this city.

Source: SFRA Architectural Advisory Panel, Mario Ciampi, “Evaluation Report: Redevelopment of the Golden Gateway,” 1960:

DEVELOPERS

SIDNEY LEIKEN ENTERPRISES
THEO G. MEYER & SONS

ARCHITECTS

JAN LUBICZ-NYCZ & ASSOCIATES

This scheme is composed of a single apartment building of cruciform plan with 33 stories stepped back from the center in striated slabs. This building contains approximately 2100 apartment units elevated over a park with parking garages below. A shopping and recreational center adjoins this central element.

The basic concept of this proposal is remarkably bold, dynamic and brilliantly provocative. A wonderfully large space in the downtown area is created and an excellent relationship with Portsmouth Square, Ferry Park, the public garage and Customs House is achieved. Located in a handsome park setting, the apartment structure is a strong sculptural statement endeavoring to capture the Telegraph Hill spirit of living environment. In concept, this structure may be said to be beyond the conventional wisdom of architecture today and would undoubtedly be a major influence on future architectural design.

The scheme, however, is decidedly preliminary in nature, with numerous inherent problems unexplored. A very serious question is raised as to the ability of achieving in final execution an excellence comparable to the original principles.

And assuredly, this outspoken structure would demand excellence in all detail.

Vehicular traffic is successfully separated from the pedestrian, and the apartments are generally very well removed from the freeway. The unit apartment plans are excellent and enjoy a privacy, a delight in the surrounding park, and magnificent views of the city and bay. The site planning of all secondary elements, how-ever, is quite weak.

The central apartment structure should lend itself to construction at reasonable cost and to apartment units of reasonable basic rentals. Vertical circulations for the 33 stories would, however, be extremely wasteful.

Despite the highly commendable freshness of this proposal, the design expression is a very personal one, largely lacking in the restraint of civic and social direction. This alone is cause for considerable concern. Moreover, there is a disturbing restlessness to the commanding structure which, together with its overwhelming scale, seems at odds with basic needs of a living environment.

This great scale, furthermore, seems particularly inappropriate to the scale of the city.

From the SFRA Architectural Advisory Panel, Mario Ciampi, “Evaluation Report: Redevelopment of the Golden Gateway,” 1960:

DEVELOPERS
BARRETT-DIVERSIFIED-LESSER-BRAEMAR

ARCHITECTS
DANIEL, MANN, JOHNSON & MENDENHALL
CORLETT & SPACKMAN

This scheme includes 9 high-rise apartment buildings, approximately 20 and 28 stories high, and a 30-story apartment building for elderly citizens, placed over the public garage. These structures spring from an elevated pedestrian plateau over the site at third floor height relative to the surrounding streets.

Two floors of parking garages and services are provided below this level.

Basic to the site planning of this proposal is the decision to ignore the city proper and relate the entire project to the freeway and harbor. This results in a very unhappy conflict with the surrounding grid pattern and a marked isolation of the project.

The pedestrian plateau is an imaginative idea with certain virtues. Three distinct levels of circulation connecting with the street pattern are created, and separation of vehicular traffic and the pedestrian is achieved. This concept could possibly be carried out in the development of surrounding areas as urban change and growth continue. The pedestrian plateau suggests, however, a bleak and barren expanse for a living environment, and provision of appropriate landscaping would present formidable considerations of structure and cost.

The shopping center is well placed and such amenities as recreation facilities have merit. However, the apartment buildings are located too closely to the elevated freeway and would be exposed to undesirable noise, night lights and confusing motion.

The high-rise apartment building for elderly citizens is most unanimously and emphatically rejected. This is particularly undesirable sociologically and psychologically.

The main structures, through their placement, size and consistency of height, somehow succeed in occupying even more space visually than physically. It would be difficult to see into or out of the canyons which are created. This prospect is made even more frightening by the absolute pervasiveness of ostentatious surfaces and bizarre forms. Projecting balconies are very exposed and would not be practical in this city.

Rather than gaining from, or lending to, the spirit of the city, this scheme loudly projects itself in sharp conflict with that spirit.

This scheme proposes 10 high-rise apartment tower units linked together in a group of 4 large modulated slab-type structures. Basement parking is provided and the city street pattern is permitted to project through the residential area.

Harrison Ryker was an early innovator in aerial photography who patented a number of surveying instruments and techniques.  In addition to his work for the U.S. Forest Service, he is known for his survey of San Francisco.  In 1938, the Works Progress Administration (a New Deal agency) hired Ryker to photograph the city from the air.  The result was 164 photographs which are here composited into a single image.  The Ryker photographs provide the most detailed record of the built environment exactly as it was on the eve of World War II.  A comparison to the modern Aerial Imagery (also under Basemaps) is instructive.  Areas of particular interest are downtown and the eastern waterfront.  From 1938 to the twenty first century, Candlestick Point extended further into the bay, rail yards gave way to stadia and a research campus, while the office landscape densified and extended South of Market.  The comparison also highlights dramatic changes in the western neighborhoods.  While the Sunset District was largely built-out in 1938, the western reaches of the Richmond District were still dominated by sand dunes.

Willard Farwell and John Kunkler, “Official Map of Chinatown in San Francisco,” Bosqui Eng. & Print Co., 1885.

Source: David Rumsey Map Collection

In 1885, the San Francisco Board of Supervisors appointed three of its members to form a special committee to investigate living conditions in Chinatown.  This map was included in the committee’s 100-page report.

Postbellum San Francisco was at the center of anti-Chinese agitation in the United States.  The most notorious expression of this movement was the Workingmen’s Party of California, a political party founded by a labor organizer and Irish immigrant named Dennis Kearny in the 1870s.  With a self-proclaimed “anti-coolie” platform, the Party argued that Chinese immigrants presented unfair competition to white labor, and advocated not only for a total halt to immigration, but also for the forceable removal of the Chinese who were already present in the United States.  But Kearney and his followers were only the most radical of what-was-in-fact a broad based movement that included not only more moderate elements of union labor, like the city’s Building Trades Council, but also intellectuals and land reformers like Henry George, also a resident of San Francisco (see Venit Shelton, especially Chapter 3).  The 1885 Board of Supervisors’ report on Chinatown–and the associated map presented here–stand as evidence that the municipal government of San Francisco was also a powerful member of the anti-Chinese movement.

The stated impetus for the report was to thoroughly document “the continued and persistent violation of the sanitary regulations in that portion of the city occupied by the Chinese” (Board of Supervisors, 160).  While conditions in Chinatown were indeed crowded and often unsanitary, the report nevertheless presented a profoundly racist and sensationalist portrait of the neighborhood.  Historians and planners have long understood that so-called slum conditions are best explained by observing the collision between poverty, on the one hand, and the scarcity of urban land, on the other.  In the nineteenth-century American city, people with limited resources had little choice but to crowd into small living quarters.  Limited resources also made upkeep of property a challenge–a circumstance that was exacerbated by unreliable urban services, like garbage collection.   But rather than focusing on how to resolve these systemic issues, real estate interests and local governments often scapegoated poor people, particularly poor people of color, by pointing to their supposed proclivities and preferences–the innate inferiority–of so-called slum dwellers.  This same reasoning was prevalent in elite New Yorkers’ observations of the tenements in the Lower East Side at the end of the nineteenth century.

The 1885 report on Chinatown is a textbook example of a municipality laying the blame for inhumane living conditions at the feet of the people who endured those conditions, and it did so in terms that were often virulently racist.   In order to illustrate the tenor of the discourse, it is useful to quote at length.  The report found that in Chinatown

it may truly be said that human beings exist under conditions (as regards their mode of life and the air they breathe) scarcely one degree above those under which the rats of our waterfront and other vermin live, breathe and have their being.  And this order of things seems inseparable from the very nature of the race, probably must be accepted as borne with–must be endured, if it cannot be cured–restricted and looked after, so far as possible, with unceasing vigilance, so that, whatever of benefit, “of degree,” even, that may be derived from such modification of the evil of the presence among us, may at   least be attained, not daring to hope that there can be any radical remedy for the great, overshadowing evil which Chinese immigration has inflicted upon this people (166).

In this wholly representative passage, “people” were the white residents of San Francisco, while Chinese were “the presence,” an “overshadowing evil” that was “scarcely one degree above” rats and vermin.  The conditions in which Chinese lived were here explained primarily by their “race proclivities” (209).  A proper reading of this report must situate it not only in San Francisco’s anti-Chinese movement, but also in the context of late nineteenth-century scientific racism, which relied upon a misreading of Darwin’s evolutionary biology to assert that non-white races were in fact an under-evolved subspecies of humanity.  Chinese were human, but only “scarcely.”

This passage highlights another persistent theme: for the committee, the root of the problem was immigration.  The report continually gestured towards the need for stringent immigration laws, but argued that until such laws could be passed, only the enactment and vigilant enforcement of new municipal laws could mitigate the conditions of Chinatown.  The committee did “disclaim any sympathy” with more radical proposals, like those advocated by Kearney, to use “physical force in any form to drive . . . [the Chinese] from among us, because . . . [the committee] do not recognize this method as in any sense a practical solution of the question as to how it is best to deal with a fully recognized public evil” (164-165).  The committee hoped that its careful study would promote “more intelligent discussion and more intelligent action than has been had before, and will go far, it is also hoped, to correct public sentiment in the East upon this all-important question” (165).

Reference to “the East” showed up often in discussions not only of race, but also of political radicalism in San Francisco.  “The East” primarily meant New York.  Twenty-first century American urbanites typically perceive the existence of intercity cultural identity contests, whether they choose to engage them or not.  San Francisco’s rivalry with Los Angeles dates to the early twentieth century, but the rivalry with New York is rooted in the city’s founding.  But while the nineteenth-century preoccupation with New York might be partly explained as an intercity cultural contest, much more was at stake.  The early development of San Francisco relied heavily on financing from New York banks, insurance companies, and real estate investors.  San Francisco elites complained of the superior attitudes of New Yorkers, but also expressed anxiety that the “East” perceived San Francisco as an instant city, a foreign and barbarous place.  This impression was not helped by the presence of a large Chinese population, but nor was it helped by the presence of Irish immigrants forming political parties, advocating labor radicalism, and baying for violence against another immigrant group.  How might New York’s perceptions have adjusted had the municipal government sided with the latter immigrant group?  So while the committee might have displayed a modicum of moderation on the question of the physical removal of Chinatown, that restraint must be understood in the context of a public relations campaign.  Cultural capital might have been at stake, but so was economic capital.

George Frederick Keller, “A Statue for Our Harbor” The Wasp, November 11, 1881. Source: Chinese Collection, Bancroft Library.
The Wasp was a satirical weekly magazine, published from 1876 to 1941. It covered much of the same subject matter as New York’s Harper’s Weekly, from a West Coast perspective, and its cartoons were very much modeled on those of Thomas Nast, the staff illustrator for Harper’s. This cartoon illustrates some of the themes that most preoccupied the editorial staff of The Wasp: Chinese immigration and San Francisco’s reputation among New Yorkers. Though the Statue of Liberty would not be erected for another five years, the project was a matter of frequent discussion in East Coast publications. So Keller here proposes that instead of a statue of lady liberty, San Francisco Bay deserved to be adorned with the figure of the “celestial,” a racist stereotype of a Chinese laborer dressed in tatters, with the telltale cue (ponytail), holding an opium pipe in his left hand, and with his right foot standing triumphantly atop a skull, presumably of a white laborer, complete with spectral eyes peering out into the conquered harbor. The rays of light emitting from the celestial’s head project a warning: “Ruin to White Labor. Disease. Immorality. Filth.” The moon overlooking the entire scene features slanted eyes and a devious smile.

Removal was off the table, so until the federal government passed more stringent immigration restrictions, the committee viewed municipal law as a bulwark.  Accordingly, the report sketched a series of proposed ordinances.  Surprisingly, this included fines for white property owners.  In the only passage that advanced a systemic critique of the economics of land, the report did identify white owners of Chinatown property as “particeps criminis [accomplices] in this great wrong against civilization” (207).  Prefiguring Jacob Riis’s critique of landlords in How the Other Lives (1890) by five years, the report noted that white property owners “had no special reason to regret the occupation of his premises by Chinese insofar as the rate of revenue derived therefrom is concerned, for that revenue, if your Committee are credibly informed, has been materially larger than could have been obtained from any other class of tenants” (207).  Riis developed this critique in his exposé of the African American tenements in New York, showing how landlords leveraged racial prejudice to create artificial scarcities of housing for minority residents.  Though Riis traded in racist tropes himself–and presented New York’s Chinatown in terms only slightly more charitable than the committee did San Francisco’s–he also showed how the conditions of the tenements were essentially the result of capitalist exploitation of poor people of color.  The San Francisco Board of Supervisors did not see the circumstance so clearly, presenting landlords only as accomplices rather than the principal antagonists, as Riis did.  But the committee did advocate that the “property-owner in Chinatown must be made to feel his responsibility in this matter before Chinatown can ever be brought to a level with common public decency” (207).  The property owner would be made to feel this responsibility through fines for overcrowding or other violations of municipal codes, and the report contemplated putting liens on properties that were out of compliance (212).

As for the other ordinances that the report sketched, the map itself provided a guide.  The main uses that the report mapped are the same that it proposed to regulate.  Prostitution was to be tightly regulated, as were Chinese laundries; “gambling dens” and “opium resorts” were to be closed.  In addition to these regulations, the report contemplated limiting the number of occupants permitted per block, using the most densely populated block outside of Chinatown–meaning the most densely populated block inhabited by whites–as the ceiling (212).  Though the report opposed physical removal, the committee did express the hope that the strict enforcement of a suite of new municipal ordinances would mean that “San Francisco will soon cease to be a paradise or even an attractive place of habitation for the Mongolian” (212).

The map is color-coded: beige indicates “General Chinese Occupancy”; pink indicates “Chinese Gambling Houses”; green is “Chinese Prostitution”; yellow indicates “Chinese Opium Resorts”; red indicates “Chinese Joss Houses” (or Chinese Temples); and blue indicates “White Prostitution.”  The key also notes that the map only covers the first floor of the buildings.  Since most of the buildings had multiple stories, the uses of the upper floors are not covered here.  Based on a reading of historic fire insurance maps, it is likely that the upper floors were primarily housing.  Notations on individual buildings give more detail as to use.  MDSE indicates Merchandise.  Depending on the amount of space available, buildings might be labeled Ch. or C., both of which are short for Chinese.  Thus “C. Gen MDSE” indicates Chinese General Merchandise.  The map highlights multiple instances of mixed use, such as “C. Fruit Stand Lodging,” and “C. Undertaker and Cigar Factory.”  “W.” indicates White occupancy, as in “W. Shooting Gallery” and “W. Light House Saloon.”

 

Further Reading

Barbara Berglund, Making San Francisco American: Cultural Frontiers in the Urban West, 1846-1906 (University of Kansas Press, 2007).

Nicholas Sean Hall, “The Wasp’s ‘Troublesome Children’: Culture, Satire, and the Anti-Chinese Movement in the American West,” California History (2013).

Jacob Riis, How the Other Half Lives: Studies Among the Tenements of New York (Scribner, 1890).

Guenter Risse, Plague, Fear, and Politics in San Francisco’s Chinatown (Johns Hopkins University Press, 2012).

Guenter Risse, Driven by Fear: Epidemics and Isolation in San Francisco’s House of Pestilence (University of Illinois Press, 2015).

metadata.description: This layer is a georeferenced image of a suggested site development plan in the Western Addition of San Francisco. This plan appears in “Replanning the Geary Area in the Western Addition” published in March 1952 by the San Francisco Department of City Planning. A scanned version of this map was georeferenced as part of the Imagined San Francisco project. This project traces the history of urban planning in San Francisco, placing special emphasis on unrealized schemes. Rather than using visual material simply to illustrate outcomes, Imagined San Francisco uses historical plans, maps, architectural renderings, and photographs to show what might have been. By enabling users to layer a series of urban plans, the project presents the city not only as a sequence of material changes, but also as a contingent process and a battleground for political power. Savvy institutional actors–like banks, developers, and many public officials–understood that in some cases to clearly articulate their interests would be to invite challenges. That means that textual sources like newspapers and municipal reports are limited in what they can tell researchers about the shape of political power. Urban plans, however, often speak volumes about interests and dynamics upon which textual sources remain silent. Mortgage lenders, for example, apparently thought it unwise to state that they wished to see a poor neighborhood cleared, to be replaced with a freeway onramp. Yet visual analysis of planning proposals makes that interest plain. So in the process of showing how the city might have looked, Imagined San Francisco also shows how political power actually was negotiated and exercised.

Home Owners’ Loan Corporation (HOLC), “Residential Security Map for San Francisco,” HOLC, 1937.

Source: National Archives II, RG195, HOLC, location 450, 68:6:2/ box 147.  Also available at Mapping Inequality.

The Home Owners’ Loan Corporation (HOLC) was created in 1933, as a part of FDR’s New Deal, for the purposes of helping to stabilize the housing market and assisting homeowners in danger of foreclosure by purchasing delinquent loans from lenders. Between 1933 and 1936, the corporation purchased 1,017,821 such loans, which amounted to 20% of all owner-occupied, nonfarm homes in the country.  Between 1936 and 1940, the HOLC conducted a survey of housing in all U.S. cities with populations of at least 40,000.  (239 cities met that criterion.) The resulting Residential Security Maps described mortgage lending risk, which was determined by weighing a number of attributes against one another. These included land use; age and condition of structures; accessibility of transportation, retail, and recreation facilities; ethnic, racial, and socioeconomic characteristics of the population; and lenders’ perceptions of the areas, among other considerations. The areas that HOLC deemed the safest bets for mortgage lending were given an “A” rating and were shaded green on the residential security maps; the next-best areas, the “B” areas, were shaded blue; the “C” areas, where cautious lending was advised, were shaded yellow; and those areas that were considered high risks for mortgage lenders were rated “D” and were shaded red.  The HOLC’s maps are often regarded as the original redlining maps–and indeed some private lenders subsequently used the maps for this purpose–but it is important to note several things.  The HOLC has already made all of its loans before it conducted the Residential Security study, meaning that the maps did not guide lending decisions for the corporation.  Moreover, the HOLC gave more loans in areas that it would later shade yellow and red on its maps, than it did to the better-rated areas.  Finally, while race was a factor in determining lending risk in San Francisco, the most important factor was mixed land use.  This accounts for the fact that only two of the seventeen red-shaded areas hosted minority communities, and wealthy areas like Nob Hill were deemed hazardous lending risks and were shaded red on the maps.

Ciampi. This project traces the history of urban planning in San Francisco, placing special emphasis on unrealized schemes. Rather than using visual material simply to illustrate outcomes, Imagined San Francisco uses historical plans, maps, architectural renderings, and photographs to show what might have been. By enabling users to layer a series of urban plans, the project presents the city not only as a sequence of material changes, but also as a contingent process and a battleground for political power. Savvy institutional actors–like banks, developers, and many public officials–understood that in some cases to clearly articulate their interests would be to invite challenges. That means that textual sources like newspapers and municipal reports are limited in what they can tell researchers about the shape of political power. Urban plans, however, often speak volumes about interests and dynamics upon which textual sources remain silent. Mortgage lenders, for example, apparently thought it unwise to state that they wished to see a poor neighborhood cleared, to be replaced with a freeway onramp. Yet visual analysis of planning proposals makes that interest plain. So in the process of showing how the city might have looked, Imagined San Francisco also shows how political power actually was negotiated and exercised.

In 1966, the architectural firm of Okamoto/Liskamm produced this urban renewal study for the San Francisco Redevelopment Agency (SFRA).  The proposal was unique among urban renewal plans for several reasons.  Unlike with previous plans in the Western Addition, Yerba Buena, and Golden Gateway areas, neighborhood-based groups had originally requested an SFRA study of the Mission, and it was those same groups that originally hired the design firm.  The proposed redevelopment area comprised 423 gross acres, or 271 net acres when street area was factored out. Rehabilitation was the treatment recommended for 70 percent of the structures within the survey area. Of the remaining 30 percent, only a small fraction would be cleared; the rest required no treatment at all. The plan called for large clearances only in the areas immediately surrounding the two planned rapid transit stations, one at Sixteenth and Mission Streets, and the other at Twenty-Fourth and Mission Streets. The plan would have cleared between eight and twelve square blocks.  In spite of the fact that neighborhood groups had originally supported an urban renewal plan for the Mission District, they would eventually oppose the Okamoto/Liskamm Plan.  Read more about the plan in the urban renewal essay.

The United States Coast Survey was the nation’s first federal scientific agency.  Thomas Jefferson established the Survey in 1807, and in 1970 the Nixon administration moved the agency’s functions to the new National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).  The original purpose of the Survey was to chart the nation’s coastal waters, making them safe for navigation.  Given this mandate, it is not surprising that the maps would provide the most reliable documentation of how San Francisco’s coastline changed through the nineteenth century.  But they also provide perhaps the best record of how the built environment expanded and changed, and even how the topography of the city was altered to accommodate development.

Imagined San Francisco includes the surveys from 1853, 1857, 1859, 1869, 1884, and 1926.  The site does not include the 1897 survey, which maps only “Magnetic Ranges for Compass Deviation,” nor the 1905 and 1941 surveys which focus on anchorage in the bay, and include few details of the city that do not appear in other maps.

From the early twentieth century through the 1950s the blocks just north of Market Street and west of the docks contained a series of low-rise buildings that served as the city’s primary produce market.  By all accounts this was a bustling district, but it was also inefficient and congested.  As San Francisco emerged from the Second World War the city’s leaders envisioned a new knowledge economy, and the produce market occupied land that had obvious value for office space as well as for high-rise housing.  Responding the increasingly influential Finance, Insurance, and Real Estate (FIRE) lobby, the San Francisco Redevelopment Agency (SFRA) targeted the area for urban renewal.

1945 photo showing congested streets in the produce market area of downtown San Francisco. Source: San Francisco Public Library, Historic Photograph Collection, Image ID: AAC-0526.

At the close of the 1950s, the SFRA announced a design competition.  They received eight serious applications, each from a major property developer teaming with an architecture firm.  The submissions were evaluated by a committee consisting mostly of high-profile architects, and one prominent mortgage banker.  The panel was chaired by Mario Ciampi, a local architect best known for the Berkeley Art Museum, and who did extensive consulting work with the SFRA and the San Francisco Department of City Planning.  Other prominent members included Minoru Yamasaki, the designer of the ill-fated twin towers of Manhattan’s World Trade Center, and Louis Kahn, perhaps best known for the designs of the Exeter Academy Library and the Salk Institute.  The panel’s role was advisory, so their final report did not rank submissions, or select a winner.  But the report leaves little doubt that they favored the scheme they discussed last, the proposal of developers Perini and Associates, partnering with the architects Wurster, Bernardi & Emmons with DeMars & Reay.   This was the proposal that the SFRA ultimately selected, an outcome that was typical of design competitions.  The submissions for the Golden Gateway design competition appear below, in the order that they appeared in the panel’s final report.

Map showing redevelopment area. From SFRA Architectural Advisory Panel, Mario Ciampi, “Evaluation Report: Redevelopment of the Golden Gateway,” 1960, page 4.

Construction began in 1962 and was completed in 1986.  The project created approximately 1,400 units of housing, 3.5 million square feet of office space, and about 12 acres of public space.  The final project includes the Alcoa Building, designed by Skidmore, Owings and Merril, and the Embarcadero Center, designed by John Portman.
